summary: The Satavahanas, called Andhras in the Puranas, rose in the Deccan in the 2nd century BCE (an older reckoning places their start in the 3rd), ruling from Pratishthana (Paithan) and later also from Amaravati in the east. Satakarni I pushed into Malwa and Vidarbha, but the western Deccan was lost to the Shaka satraps until Gautamiputra Satakarni won it back, beginning a long contest between the two powers. After a last revival under Yajna Sri Satakarni, the realm broke up c. 224 CE among the Abhiras, Ikshvakus, Chutus and Pallavas.
details: The Satavahanas were a Deccan family whose homeland is still argued over: some scholars place it in Andhra, others around Pratishthana in Maharashtra or in northern Karnataka. The Puranas say the founder, Simuka, overthrew the last Kanva rulers and reigned for 23 years. An inscription at the Buddhist stupa of Kanaganahalli, on the Bhima river, mentions year 16 of Simuka and is dated to about 110 BCE. Most modern historians use evidence like this to start the dynasty in the late 2nd century BCE, though an older 'long chronology' pushes it back to the 3rd century BCE.

Simuka was followed by his brother Kanha (Krishna). He carried Satavahana rule westward to Nashik, on the upper Godavari, a town on the routes between the Deccan plateau and the ports of the Konkan coast. An inscription in Cave 19 of the Pandavleni caves near Nashik dates to his reign and is one of the earliest records of the dynasty. Holding Nashik gave the Satavahanas a foothold in the western Deccan, the region they would fight over with rival powers for the next three centuries.

Satakarni I, the third king, was the first great conqueror of the line. Taking advantage of turmoil among the Indo-Greeks and other northern powers, he seized western Malwa, Anupa in the Narmada valley and Vidarbha in the east. His widow Nayanika later recorded his reign in an inscription in the Naneghat pass, on the trade route from Junnar down to the coast, listing the costly Vedic rites he performed, including the Ashvamedha horse sacrifice and the Rajasuya, both claims to supreme kingship. The Kalinga king Kharavela also names him, though scholars disagree over whether the two ever fought.

His successor, usually identified as Satakarni II, is said to have reigned for 56 years. He captured eastern Malwa from the declining Shunga dynasty, carrying Satavahana power north of the Narmada into central India. An inscription on the southern gateway of the great Buddhist stupa at Sanchi records a gift made under a 'King Satakarni', most probably this king, and is dated to between about 50 BCE and the turn of the era. The Satavahanas now held a wide belt of land across the northern and western Deccan.

In the 1st century CE the Western Kshatrapas, Shaka rulers of Gujarat and Malwa, took the Satavahanas' western lands, and their king Nahapana ruled around Nashik and Pune through his son-in-law Rishabhadatta. Gautamiputra Satakarni struck back and defeated him. In the Jogalthembi hoard, found in Nashik district, many of Nahapana's silver coins were restruck with Gautamiputra's name. The date is disputed: some scholars place the victory in 78 CE, others around 124 CE, and his reign is dated anywhere from c. 60–85 to c. 106–130. Either way, the western Deccan returned to Satavahana rule.

Gautamiputra's son Vasishthiputra Pulumavi kept his father's lands and added the Bellary region in the south. In Pulumavi's 19th regnal year, Gautamiputra's mother, Gautami Balashri, dedicated Cave 3 at the Pandavleni caves near Nashik to Buddhist monks, with a long inscription praising her son. It claims Gautamiputra ruled from Malwa and Saurashtra to the Krishna river and from the Konkan to Vidarbha, that he destroyed the Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas, and that his horses drank from three oceans. Historians treat the boast with caution; his hold on the far north-west was probably short-lived.

The Western Kshatrapas recovered under Rudradaman I, who ruled c. 130–150. His Sanskrit inscription on a rock at Junagadh in Gujarat, dated 150 CE, boasts that he twice defeated Satakarni, 'lord of Dakshinapatha' (the Deccan), in fair fight but spared him because they were closely related: Rudradaman had given a daughter in marriage to a Satavahana prince. Which Satakarni he meant is still argued over. Rudradaman won back most of Nahapana's old lands except the area around Pune and Nashik, and the Satavahanas were pushed back onto the Deccan and their eastern lands around Amaravati.

Yajna Sri Satakarni, who reigned from roughly the 170s to the 190s, was the last strong king of the main line. He won back territory from the Western Kshatrapas and issued silver coins copying theirs, a sign that he now controlled lands where satrap money had circulated. His inscriptions at Nashik and Kanheri in the west and in the Guntur region in the east show him ruling across the whole Deccan from sea to sea. Some of his coins carry the image of a ship, pointing to the importance of seaborne trade.

Yajna Sri's revival did not last. Late in his reign the Abhiras captured the northern parts of the Satavahana realm around Nashik. The loss cut the dynasty off from the western routes and ports that had brought it so much wealth. After Yajna Sri, a series of short-lived kings, including Madhariputra Isvarasena, Vijaya and Vasishthiputra Chadha Satakarni, ruled a shrinking kingdom whose centre moved steadily east, towards the lower Krishna valley in Andhra. Nashik, once the heart of Satavahana power in the west, would not be recovered.

Pulumavi IV is counted as the last king of the main Satavahana line, reigning from about 217 to about 224. His power was concentrated in the eastern Deccan, in the lower Krishna valley. The region was rich, and during his reign Buddhist monuments were being built at Nagarjunakonda and Amaravati, among the great Buddhist centres of ancient India. But royal authority over the outlying provinces had weakened, and local families who had governed in the name of the Satavahanas were ready to rule in their own right.

Around 224–225 the Satavahana state broke apart. Its western part around Nashik went to the Abhiras, the Krishna–Guntur region in the east to the Andhra Ikshvakus, and northern Karnataka to the Chutus of Banavasi, while the Pallavas rose in the south-east around Kanchi. A collateral Satavahana branch survived in the north until the early 4th century. The Western Kshatrapas, the Satavahanas' old rivals in the west, outlived them by about two centuries, until the Gupta Empire brought their rule to an end.
